Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Gameplay 2.1 1. Place a Tile 2.2 2. Place a Meeple (optional) 2.3 3. Score (if feature is completed) 3 Game End and Final Scoring 4 Variants 4.1 The River 4.2 Inns & Cathedrals (Expansion 1) 4.3 Traders & Builders (Expansion 2) 4.4 The Princess & the Dragon (Expansion 3) Overview Carcassonne is a tile-placement game. Players take turns expanding the landscape of roads, cities, monasteries, and fields, one tile at a time, to build the city of Carcassonne. Meeples are used to occupy various features. The player(s) with the most meeples on a feature score points. Gameplay 1. Place a Tile On your turn, you must place a tile in such a way that it continues the landscape features of any tiles it touches. BGA will prevent you from placing a tile adjacent to any incompatible tiles. Each of the four edges of the tile will have one of three features: City, Road, or Farm. Monastery only appears in the center of a tile. 2. Place a Meeple (optional) You can place a meeple somewhere on the tile. It stays on that tile until that feature is scored. You cannot place a meeple on a feature that already has other meeples. But you can get multiple meeples on a single feature if they start them as separate features, then later a tile is placed that joins them. 3. Score (if feature is completed) Scoring occurs only when a feature is completed or when there are no more tiles to place (i.e., the game ends). Only the player who has a meeple occupying the feature can score. If the feature has more than one meeple, the player with the most meeples on that feature gets the points. In ties, each player gets full points. When a feature is completed and scored, the meeples on it return to their players' supply. Feature Image Completion Criteria Score Term for occupant Road Each end must meet a village, a city, a monastery, or loop back onto itself. Each tile of the road grants 1 VP. Highwayman City Every side has a wall with no gaps inside. Cities cannot be joined corner to corner. 2 VP per tile + 2 VP per blue shield (coat of arms) in the city. Knight Monastery Surrounded by tiles on all sides and corners (8 tiles). 9 points (one per tile surrounding the monastery plus the monastery itself). Monk Game End and Final Scoring The game ends when a player can no longer take or place a tile. At that point, incomplete features with meeples on them are scored. Feature Image Score for incomplete feature Road Each tile of the road grants 1 point. City 1 point per tile + 1 point per blue shield (coat of arms) Monastery Each tile surrounding the monastery, plus the monastery itself, is worth 1 point. Farm 3 points per completed city that touches the field. Variants The River In The River variant, all river tiles are played first, creating one long river from which to start the rest of the game. Inns & Cathedrals (Expansion 1) This expansion includes city tiles with cathedrals and road tiles with inns , plus large meeples. A completed road with an inn on it scores 2 VP per tile (final scoring is still 1 VP per tile for an incomplete road). A completed city with a cathedral in it scores 3 VP per tile (final scoring is still 1 VP per tile for an incomplete city). You may choose to place a large meeple on a feature. A large meeple counts as 2 regular meeples when deciding who controls the feature. Large meeples don't change how the feature is scored. Traders & Builders (Expansion 2) This expansion includes goods tokens, builder meeples, and pig meeples. When you place a meeple on a road or city , you may also add the builder meeple. If you place a tile that adds to the road or city that the builder is occupying, you may take a second turn. Then the builder is returned to your supply. Builders do not count toward feature control or scoring. When you place a meeple in a field , you may also add the pig meeple. If you complete a city with at least 1 blue shield, you score 3 points for each completed city touching the field with your pig. Feature control is not a factor--all players with pigs score. Pigs do not count toward feature control or final scoring. If you complete a city , for each goods symbol shown in that city, you receive 1 corresponding goods token. It does not matter if you have a meeple occupying that city or not. The city scores as normal. During final scoring, if you have collected the most goods of that type, you score 10 points. The Princess & the Dragon (Expansion 3) This expansion puts Carcassonne in the world of high fantasy, with dragons, fairies, and magic portals. When playing a tile with a magic portal on it , you may place a meeple on any tile that has already been played (following normal placement rules). When you play a tile with a princess on it to an existing city, you may remove another player's meeple from that city instead of placing one of your own. When you play a tile with a volcano on it , immediately add the dragon to this tile. Meeples cannot be placed on a volcano. When you play a tile with a dragon on it , players take turns moving the dragon meeple until it moves 6 times or cannot move. The dragon must move orthogonally, not diagonally (only north, south, east, or west). Any meeples on tiles the dragon visits are eaten and replaced in the player's supply. The dragon cannot visit the same tile twice in the same turn (no backtracking). The dragon cannot visit the tile with the fairy. Meeples cannot be placed on the same tiles as the dragon. If the dragon is not on the game board (i.e., no volcano tiles have been played), this icon is ignored. If you cannot or choose not to add/move a meeple to any tile, you may instead move the fairy meeple to one of your meeples. If the fairy is still assigned to your meeple at the start of your turn, you immediately score 1 VP. If your meeple and the fairy are on a tile when its feature is completed, you get 3 VP, regardless of whether you control the feature. The dragon cannot enter a tile with the fairy on it. All figures on the fairy's tile are protected from the dragon's hunger.

---

Carcassonne is a tile placement game in which the players draw and place a tile with a piece of southern French landscape represented on it. The tile might feature a city, a road, a cloister, grassland or some combination thereof, and it must be placed adjacent to tiles that have already been played, in such a way that cities are connected to cities, roads to roads, et cetera. Having placed a tile, the player can then decide to place one of their meeples in one of the areas on it: in the city as a knight, on the road as a robber, in the cloister as a monk, or in the field as a farmer. When that area is complete that meeple scores points for its owner.

During a game of Carcassonne, players are faced with decisions like: "Is it really worth putting my last meeple there?" or "Should I use this tile to expand my city, or should I place it near my opponent instead, thus making it a harder for them to complete it and score points?" Since players place only one tile and have the option to place one meeple on it, turns proceed quickly even if it is a game full of options and possibilities.

First game in the Carcassonne series.
community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] There are 3 games I avoid like the plague - Catan, Puerto Rico and Carcassonne. The pieces are crap, the gameplay stunted and the game objective a joke. I mean, what's the significance of a place like Carcassonne in human history that they gotta make a game about it? A real waste of time, and completely pointless to boot. Even when you've emerged victorious, you don't feel like you actually did anything to deserve victory. I know the Germans are trying hard to stay away from violent themes in boardgaming, but this is absolutely ridiculous. Watching paint dry might be more fun by comparson.

[Rating: 1/10] Wow, this game really is not fun.  For some reason I kept getting suckered into playing this.  It looks cool and seems like it should be up my alley, but it reminds me of Trivial Pursuit.  You always want what the other people get and you get screwed when it comes to you.  Too random.  I will not play this again, ever!  Warning: Not broken on its own, needs the Morgan expansion to destroy all game playability.

[Rating: 1/10] Played this several times, base game and version with many many expansions - and every time I was bored after the first 5 minutes.  This game has neither strategy nor tactic to consider. Just draw a random tile, place it where it might potentially help you and not help or hinder the opponent, place one of your pieces if you want and you are done.  Unless you memorized all the tiles and know how many "outs" are still in the stacks this is a completely random game.  bbb

[Rating: 1/10] Ugh! Why do so many people love this game? Honestly, to me, this is a bland nothing of a game, typical of so many Eurotrash games. The theme, such as it is, makes no sense, the artwork is uninspiring and the gameplay is pedestrian. If I had a choice between spending an hour playing this and staring at a wall for an hour, I'd feel more entertained staring at the wall.
